title: Column generation (Branch-and-Price, ch. 2, pp. 43–102)
contribution: Expository chapter giving one notation for master, pricing and later Dantzig–Wolfe, the objects/representations/encodings vocabulary, and practical rules for initialization, column management, heuristic pricing and tolerances, with six worked applications and twenty exercises; only the hypergeometric evaluation of degenerate pivots is claimed as new (pp. 5–60, 52).
problem_entry: Starts from the general stance of dropping a hurdle and working back to it; column generation does this for too many variables, is kept apart from Dantzig–Wolfe, and is said to be uncompetitive for pure LP but a winner in IP (pp. 3–4).
key_idea: Column generation is primal simplex with pricing as an optimization over implicit X; master and pricing talk only through π; five presentation changes: λ_x indexing, object→representation→encoding triad, zero object, heuristic pricing as standard, textbook/simple/advanced comparison (pp. 5–17, 27–28).
assumptions: Master LP over finite huge X, feasible with finite optimum, λ ≥ 0 only; upper bounds on λ advised against; encodings must preserve addition and scaling (non-linear costs deferred to §4.5); bounds need κ^k, Corollary 2.2 needs |K|=1 and c_x=1, Farley needs c_x ≥ 0 (pp. 5, 13, 19–21).
proof_devices: Proposition 2.1 bound via splitting the objective into reduced cost plus π^T a ((2.12)–(2.14), p. 19)
Corollary 2.2 via dual feasibility of π/(1 − c̄(π)) (p. 20)
Farley's bound via dual feasibility of l(π)·π (pp. 20–21)
Note 2.17: bounds survive under-approximation of the minimum reduced cost; heuristic or partial pricing gives no bound (p. 20)
Note 2.6: last iteration returns c̄(π) = 0 by complementary slackness (p. 8)
Hypergeometric estimate of degenerate pivots (p. 22; Exercise 2.19, pp. 59–60)
experiments: Illustration only: one VRPTW instance (Fig. 2.4, optimum at iteration 736, proven at 952) and Table 2.1 textbook/simple/advanced at one root node (2,111.7 s vs 46.9 s vs 105.7 s) with Irnich's code; no instance, hardware, solver version or variability stated (pp. 21–28, 51).
positioning: Continues Lübbecke and Desrosiers (2005); corrects history crediting Kantorovich–Zalgaller (1951) via Uchoa and Sadykov (2024); names schools and software (SCIP, BaPCod/Coluna; GCG not named); corrects misconceptions directly (pp. 4, 16, 40, 49–51).
writing: Three layers (core / Good to Know / More to Know), playful numbered Notes, direct questions to the reader, hedges where knowledge stops, one proposition and three corollaries with intuitive readings, twenty exercises (pp. 1–60).
limits_future: Open: effects of upper bounds (p. 5), which RMP solver gives useful duals (p. 16), perturbation size (p. 24), cost per column vs per iteration (p. 28), parallel pricing (p. 51); tailing-off and stabilization handed to ch. 6 (pp. 22–23).

method_links.note: Joint voice: the 2005 survey is the spine of §2.1; the Kantorovich attribution is corrected with credit to Uchoa and Sadykov (step 6); points that cannot be stated exactly are printed as open (step 4).

Steps 4 and 6: balancing master and pricing time is the stated guideline and the pricing time share is reported; integrality imposed on original arc-flow variables in the aircraft-routing IMP; the single-depot problem is admitted easy as network flow and set-partitioned only for teaching.
Enumeration of tiny instances as a teaching device: the reader lists every pricing solution, every IMP optimum and every extreme point of conv(X).

Numbers from one unnamed root node with no hardware or solver version carry the general wording 'tremendous results', the gap Method 3 step 6 guards against; Note 2.15 itself says the RMP solver's effect on pricing should be tested.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Numerical care at the master–subproblem interface
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Equal RMP and pricing tolerances, rounding columns at the pricing integrality tolerance; qualifies SKILL.md's Honest Boundary on numerics, at least for the joint book.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Select for diversity, not by score alone
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Never select columns by reduced cost alone; complementary or orthogonal columns.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Decode back to the owner's objects
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Object→representation→encoding triad; store x with its encoding.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: After a primal trick, ask for its dual analogue
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A GENCOL programmer's ±2-minute tolerance led to Desrosiers's question, which started stabilized column generation.

transferable: Index master variables by their pricing solutions so that master, pricing and later reformulation share one notation (Note 2.3, p. 5).
Initialize with Farkas pricing: zero costs and the dual ray as the pricing objective, with no big-M to tune (pp. 10–11).
Keep one optimality tolerance for RMP and pricing. Round new columns at the pricing solver's integrality tolerance and recompute their reduced cost before adding them (p. 24).
Price in a cascade: pool, then restricted or truncated pricing, and exact pricing only to prove optimality. Log when no valid lower bound is available, as under partial pricing (pp. 17–18, 20, 28).
Select returned columns for diversity (complementary or orthogonal paths), pool the rest and cap the RMP at about 3m columns (pp. 16, 41–42).
Stop column generation on a relative gap, using ⌈LB⌉ for integer objectives, and branch (Note 2.18, p. 23).
Add a zero object (a binary x_0 or a reverse depot arc) so that doing nothing is a zero-cost, zero-column pricing solution (pp. 31–32, 41).
Keep set-partitioning upper bounds implicit in the master LP (pp. 5, 17).
Rescale column coefficients (times relative to the window, not the week) to reduce simplex instability (p. 48).
Report a textbook / simple / advanced table with iterations, columns, time, share of time in pricing, bound and gap (p. 27).
coauthors: Jacques Desrosiers, Guy Desaulniers, Jean Bertrand Gauthier

quotes.text: ideally, one needs to solve the pricing problem to optimality only once, in the last column generation iteration, to prove optimality of the MP.
The heavy-work and creativity actually begin after we have a functional textbook implementation.

title: Integrated Topology and Redispatch Optimization of Real-World Power Transmission Systems using Branch-and-Benders-Cut
contribution: Gives a full SCOTS formulation with N-1 security and a branch-and-Benders-cut algorithm with integrated components (SLE-U subproblems, subproblem selection, cut filtering, partial decomposition, connectivity handling, heuristic), evaluated on synthetic and real German grid instances, with the software TopologyOptimizer.jl (§§2–5, p. 28).
problem_entry: Application entry: congestion management costs billions and topology is handled manually; the compact MILP replicates DC flow per contingency and exceeds workstation memory on national grids, ruling out a monolithic solve (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Benders along contingencies with lazy cuts in the MILP tree; subproblems as linear systems on a contracted graph with rank-1 LU updates (SLE-U), scored subproblem selection, cut filtering, base case in the master, bridge-based connectivity cuts, restricted-switching heuristic; re-profile to aim each next component (pp. 13–23).
assumptions: MILP with binaries, integers and continuous flows and big-M Kirchhoff constraints; lossless DC with angle bounds; N-1 set incl. base case; multi-period coupling; substation arcs equalize angles; islanding-free; uniqueness of fixed-network flow; synthetic PGLib-derived data lacking several groups; real data confidential (pp. 6–13, 15, 22, 25, 28).
proof_devices: No theorems; uniqueness of the fixed-network power-flow linear system (Birkhoff and Diaz 1956) (p. 15)
Rank-1 LU update complexity count, O(|A|·|V|³) to O(|A|·|V|²) (pp. 15–17)
experiments: 130 synthetic instances (31 separate for tuning), Z=1, 3 h limit, stated hardware and Gurobi 13.0.2/Julia; ablation chain Table 2 by solved count and shifted geometric mean (compact 110 solved, 534.37 s, down to 36.86 s); practical study Z=1…5; real world 71 days × 24 h with an older version and AC checks; single run, no seeds (pp. 22–26).
positioning: Placed against OTS/SCOTS, substation reconfiguration, formulation work, Benders for UC and partial Benders, heuristics; Table 1 scope-and-status comparison with only Kocuk et al. (2016) and this work exact; hedged novelty; builds on companion papers; Gurobi a partner (pp. 2–5, 29).
writing: Three numbered scoped contributions, sources in constraint-group headers, an Implementation scope paragraph, negative sentences on what results do not establish, a rounding quirk in percentages, back matter with CRediT and generative-AI declaration, inconsistent code-availability statements (pp. 3, 5–6, 13, 22–28).
limits_future: DC not AC-feasible, gains not comparable to TSO actions, older version in real runs, synthetic data lacks substations, gaps widen with Z, hours sequential, human in the loop; conclusion overreaches on provable optimality and model flexibility; future: open source, curative measures, expansion planning (pp. 13, 22–28).

method_links.note: Compact model kept as row 1 (110 of 130, 534.37 s); its memory limit on national grids is the stated reason to decompose; master time share 7.60% → 51.90% read to aim the next components (step 4, after the build).

Benders along contingencies chosen for memory and time, not a Dantzig–Wolfe bound gain, so no root-bound go/no-go or pre-build probe; built on Gurobi with lazy cuts in Julia/JuMP, not SCIP; partial decomposition keeps the base case in the master (−8.40%) as the Benders analogue of step 6.

Identical conditions and a separate tuning set; ablation chain with predecessor column, solved counts, shifted geometric mean with its shift, failures charged, performance profile; losses reported; uneven comparison flagged; real-world claims bounded.

No external SCOTS method re-run (Table 1 compares scope only); synthetic public benchmark because real data are confidential; randomness but no seeds and a single run; 'statistically significant' without a test; two conclusion claims wider than the tables.

Exact optima counted against a heuristic's premise (18 of 107; 28 of 107); scores of §§3.3 and 3.5 described in detail but the tuned settings are random order and base case only and losing variants are not tabulated: a proxy that looks right is not evidence.
Synthesis as the contribution of a model rather than a survey: scattered constraint groups collected into one formulation with their sources in the paragraph headers.

transferable: Build the evaluation as a component chain: each row names its predecessor and gives solved count, mean and shifted geometric mean, with the shift and the time charged to failures stated. Put the compact model in row 1 and add a performance profile (Table 2, pp. 22–23).
Tune every parameter on an instance set kept separate from the benchmark (31 against 130, p. 22).
After each component, re-measure the master's share of time and aim the next component at the new bottleneck (p. 23).

For a flow model with fixed topology, solve Benders subproblems as linear systems on the contracted graph, and update the LU factorization by rank-1 steps between subproblems instead of re-solving LPs (pp. 15–17).
Solve only a scored or random subset of subproblems per iteration, with periodic full rounds. Filter cuts by violation under absolute, relative and gap-share caps, always keeping one (pp. 17–19).
Partial decomposition: keep the base-case flow in the master before trying contingency flows (pp. 19, 23).
Reuse one subproblem template per worker and change only the contingency-dependent rows (p. 14).
Argue for integrated optimization with counts of exact optima that break a heuristic's premise (18 of 107; 28 of 107, p. 26).
Count an improvement only above a stated absolute threshold, to filter numerical noise (p. 23).
For real-world claims, write what the evidence does not establish and say when the reported algorithm version differs (pp. 25–26).
Position against prior work with a scope-and-status table, and define *exact* in its note (Table 1, p. 5).

quotes.text: The contribution here lies mainly in the full collection of constraints rather than any individual set of constraints.
These results therefore do not establish additional redispatch cost savings over current practice.
